title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with a synthetic likeness, not a model that merely got a fact wrong. Someone placed a video call over a consumer messaging app using an AI-generated deepfake of a sitting chief minister, and the fabricated face was the credential that made the rest of the approach credible. The fraud then ran on ordinary social engineering: a supposed manager, a supposed CBI officer, escalating fees, and payments made voluntarily by the target through a digital payment app. No part of the chain depended on breaking a system. It depended on a person believing what a screen showed him.

The failure sits at the point where identity is asserted and never verified. A video call carries no proof that the face on it belongs to the person it resembles, and the payment app carries no check on why the money is being sent. Catching this would have required confirming the caller's identity through a channel the caller does not control, or a check at the transfer stage that flagged a private individual sending repeated payments to unlock a promised government benefit. Neither existed here, and the reporting describes no technical safeguard that failed, only safeguards that were absent.

What is not established is who made the call or what tools generated the likeness. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act and police issued a warning, which is a complaint and an investigation, not a finding against any named person. The report also comes from a single outlet, and its account of the call rests on the complainant's description.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A Bengaluru security guard, Ratikanta Giri, 29, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on Sept 9 from someone using an AI generated deepfake of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay. The caller claimed to offer financial aid and promised Rs 11 lakh, saying it would come through a foreign account in dollars. A supposed manager then told Giri that Rs 5 lakh was allotted and asked for fees. This was the city's first reported case of its kind.

Giri was asked to pay Rs 5,000 as exchange charges, then Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN, and more after a person posing as a CBI officer demanded over Rs 50,000 as a fine. He transferred over Rs 1.04 lakh in total through a digital payment app. When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he had been cheated. He called the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then approached Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act, and police warned people not to trust such calls or make payments.
